source.title: Generalization Properties of Stochastic Optimizers via Trajectory Analysis
source.authors: Liam Hodgkinson; Umut Simsekli; Rajiv Khanna; Michael W. Mahoney

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some mathematical notation is garbled in the supplied extraction, but the empirical findings and their descriptions are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures optimizer-trajectory properties and their association with generalization error using lower-tail exponents and the Fernique–Talagrand functional, different measures from the claim versions’ specified experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports correlations between lower-tail exponents and generalization gap, and between the Fernique–Talagrand functional and test error. These results bear on measured properties tracking generalization, but do not test the specific magnitude-aware sharpness measure or experiments described in V1–V8. Figures 2, 5, and 6 provide plots without extractable per-setting numeric values.
record.test_reason: The study tests trajectory-based predictors of generalization, but none of V1–V8. Lower-tail exponents and Fernique–Talagrand functionals are different constructs from V7's magnitude-aware sharpness. Using multiple architectures and batch sizes does not itself establish the comparisons specified by V3 or V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors derive trajectory-based generalization bounds and connect them to lower-tail exponents through a local random-walk approximation. Their experiments report correlations rather than causal evidence; they explicitly leave universality and confounding by optimizer hyperparameters unresolved.
record.recipe_differences: The study develops and evaluates trajectory-based measures (lower-tail exponents and the Fernique–Talagrand functional); it does not reproduce the interventions or measurements specified in the versions.
record.method_sensitivity: The estimated lower-tail exponent varies monotonically with the step-size-to-batch-size ratio. The authors note that the correlation between lower-tail exponent and generalization gap may arise from shared dependence on optimizer hyperparameters.

fits_no_version.finding: Estimated lower-tail exponents correlate positively with generalization gaps across the tested image-model configurations, with reported p-values from 10^-12 to 10^-4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower-tail exponents of SGD trajectories correlate with generalization gaps in these settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Lower-tail exponents vary monotonically with the learning-rate-to-batch-size ratio; reported p-values range from 10^-9 to 10^-3.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SGD hyperparameters are associated with the lower-tail behavior of its local transition kernel.

fits_no_version.finding: For synthetic random walks normalized by coordinate-wise standard deviation, the estimated FT functional increases with the prescribed lower-tail exponent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Lower-tail exponents track the normalized FT functional in the tested synthetic processes.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors report a strong association between the estimated FT functional and end-of-training test error in Wine Quality regression.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The trajectory FT functional correlates with held-out regression error in the tested small-network setting.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of the 39th International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 162, 2022
record.problems: The neural-network experiments use simple models and two image datasets. Lower-tail exponent estimation is described as challenging and less reliable for fitted α values greater than approximately 5. The authors state that the observed correlation may reflect correlations between the exponent and optimizer hyperparameters, and that universality is untested. Several findings are shown only in figures, without per-setting values in the text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting versus natural-label and random-label held-out accuracy.
Test error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected test error and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer performance under specified tuning conditions.
Large-batch held-out penalties in image classifiers or language models under fixed epoch budgets, and remedies.
Dropout's effect on held-out error and its interactions with dataset size, augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its relationship to generalization gaps, and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized examples versus equally many random examples and retraining.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to V1–V8 because the rows measure different constructs, not because the reported adjacent effects are absent. No version-specific verdict is warranted. Appendix B's qualitative discussion connecting flatness to trajectory variance does not test magnitude-aware sharpness.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweep past interpolation on natural labels.
Convolutional versus fully connected image generalization comparisons.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD, including tuning and optimizer-switch conditions.
Large-batch generalization penalties under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout and weight-decay effects on held-out error.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparisons with norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring the effect on test accuracy.

rows.subject: FCN5, FCN7, and CNN9
rows.size_stated: FCN5 and FCN7 have 5 and 7 layers; CNN9 has 9 layers; other size not stated
rows.stage_stated: trained with constant step-size SGD until training accuracy reaches exactly 100%, then run 200 additional iterations
rows.operation_detail: Relate estimated lower-tail exponent of the post-training trajectory to generalization gap across configurations.

conditions.value: without weight-decay or momentum; no data augmentation stated

rows.measure: Association of estimated lower-tail exponent α with generalization gap
rows.value: Figure only; text reports positive correlations in all configurations, with p-values ranging from 10⁻¹² to 10⁻⁴ under a linear model.
rows.note: The text describes a positive, significant association across configurations but does not give per-architecture, per-dataset, or per-configuration values.
rows.check: The positive exponent–gap correlation is reported correctly, but it does not measure any claim version. Its significance does not establish the magnitude-aware sharpness relationship in V7.

rows.subject: FCN5, FCN7, and CNN9
rows.size_stated: FCN5 and FCN7 have 5 and 7 layers; CNN9 has 9 layers; other size not stated
rows.stage_stated: trained with constant step-size SGD until training accuracy reaches exactly 100%, then run 200 additional iterations
rows.operation_detail: Relate estimated lower-tail exponent α to step-size divided by batch-size.
rows.measure: Association of lower-tail exponent α with η/b
rows.value: Figure only; text reports clear monotonicity.
rows.note: This result describes a hyperparameter association, not a direct generalization-gap comparison.
rows.check: This measures an exponent–hyperparameter association, not held-out performance under fixed epoch budgets. Figure 3 reports linear-model p-values from 10^-9 to 10^-3, which should replace the unspecified uncertainty.

rows.subject: Random walks with prescribed lower-tail exponents
rows.operation_detail: Measure normalized Fernique–Talagrand functional as the prescribed lower-tail exponent varies.

conditions.value: chain normalized by coordinate-wise standard deviation

rows.measure: Normalized Fernique–Talagrand functional γ₂ρ of the trajectory
rows.value: Figure only; text says the functional grows with α and appears to grow like log α for small α.
rows.note: This is a toy-process result on a trajectory functional, not a neural-network generalization-gap measurement.
rows.check: The subject is a synthetic random walk, not a toy neural network. Figure 5 specifies shaded 95% confidence intervals across 100 runs; the record incorrectly says the confidence interval is unspecified. No predictive generalization is measured.

rows.subject: Three-layer fully-connected neural network with 20 hidden units
rows.stage_stated: trained for 30 epochs from the same random initialization; text says this is before reaching 100% training accuracy
rows.operation_detail: Compare test error at the end of training with the normalized Fernique–Talagrand functional estimated from the final 50 iterates.
rows.measure: Association between estimated normalized Fernique–Talagrand functional and test error
rows.value: Figure only; text reports a strong correlation to test error, with the most profound difference in trends seen with varying batch size.
rows.note: The text does not specify the direction or numerical strength of the association.
rows.check: Wine Quality regression does not test V5's image-classification or language-model claim. The input-noise condition also confuses standard deviation with variance: sigma is 0, 0.05, or 0.1, giving variances 0, 0.0025, or 0.01. The prose describes test error, although Figure 6's caption calls the outcome generalization gap; preserve that ambiguity.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
